claim: TET enzymes convert 5-methylcytosine (5mC) into 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC).
source: The conversion of 5-methylcytosine (5mC) into 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) initiates developmental and cell-type-specific transcriptional programs through mechanisms that include changes in the chromatin structure.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known function of TET enzymes.

claim: The presence of 5hmC in transcribed genes promotes the annealing of nascent RNA to the template DNA strand, leading to R-loop formation.
source: Here, we show that the presence of 5hmC in the transcribed gene promotes the annealing of the nascent RNA to the template DNA strand, leading to the formation of an R-loop.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: Depletion of TET enzymes reduced global R-loops in the absence of gene expression changes.
source: Depletion of TET enzymes reduced global R-loops in the absence of gene expression changes
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: CRISPR-mediated tethering of TET to an active gene promoted the formation of R-loops.
source: whereas CRISPR-mediated tethering of TET to an active gene promoted the formation of R-loops.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2E-F.

claim: The genome-wide distribution of 5hmC and R-loops shows a positive correlation in mouse and human stem cells.
source: The genome-wide distribution of 5hmC and R-loops shows a positive correlation in mouse and human stem cells
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: 5hmC and R-loops overlap in half of all active genes.
source: overlap in half of all active genes
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and quantified in Figure 3D showing 51% overlap.

claim: R-loop resolution leads to differential expression of a subset of genes involved in crucial events during stem cell proliferation.
source: Moreover, R-loop resolution leads to differential expression of a subset of genes that are involved in crucial events during stem cell proliferation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RNA-seq analysis in Figure 6.

claim: R-loops are physiologically relevant intermediates of several processes, such as immunoglobulin class-switch recombination and gene expression.
source: These triple-stranded structures, called R-loops, are physiologically relevant intermediates of several processes, such as immunoglobulin class-switch recombination and gene expression (García-Muse and Aguilera, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Nonscheduled or persistent R-loops constitute an important source of DNA damage, namely DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs).
source: However, nonscheduled or persistent R-loops constitute an important source of DNA damage, namely, DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) (García-Muse and Aguilera, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: RNase H1 and RNase H2 degrade R-loops by digesting the RNA strand of the DNA:RNA hybrid.
source: The ribonuclease H enzymes RNase H1 and RNase H2 degrade R-loops by digesting the RNA strand of the DNA:RNA hybrid.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: DNA and RNA helicases unwind the hybrid and restore the double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) structure.
source: DNA and RNA helicases unwind the hybrid and restore the double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) structure.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: DDX23 resolves R-loops formed during transcription elongation to regulate gene expression programs and prevent transcription-dependent DNA damage.
source: For instance, we previously reported that the DEAD-box helicase 23 (DDX23) resolves R-loops formed during transcription elongation to regulate gene expression programs and prevent transcription-dependent DNA damage (Sridhara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The presence of introns prevents unscheduled R-loop formation at active genes.
source: The presence of introns, for instance, prevents unscheduled R-loop formation at active genes (Bonnet et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: An asymmetrical distribution of guanines (G) and cytosines (C) nucleotides in the DNA duplex influences R-loop propensity, with an excess of Cs in the template DNA strand (positive G:C skew) favoring R-loop formation.
source: An asymmetrical distribution of guanines (G) and cytosines (C) nucleotides in the DNA duplex also influences R-loop propensity, with an excess of Cs in the template DNA strand (positive G:C skew) favoring R-loop formation (Ginno et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Promoter-proximal R-loops enhance the recruitment of the Tip60–p400 histone acetyltransferase complex and inhibit the binding of polycomb-repressive complex 2 and histone H3 lysine-27 methylation.
source: Promoter-proximal R-loops enhance the recruitment of the Tip60–p400 histone acetyltransferase complex and inhibit the binding of polycomb-repressive complex 2 and histone H3 lysine-27 methylation (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: R-loops formed over G-rich terminator elements promote histone H3 lysine-9 dimethylation, a repressive mark that reinforces RNA polymerase II pausing during transcription termination.
source: R-loops formed over G-rich terminator elements promote histone H3 lysine-9 dimethylation, a repressive mark that reinforces RNA polymerase II pausing during transcription termination (Skourti-Stathaki and Proudfoot, 2014; Chédin, 2016; Skourti-Stathaki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: R-loops act as barriers against DNA methylation spreading into active genes.
source: Besides affecting histone modifications, R-loops also act as barriers against DNA methylation spreading into active genes (Ginno et al., 2013; Ginno et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: More than 70% of all human gene promoters contain stretches of CpG dinucleotides, termed CpG islands (CGIs), whose transcriptional activity is repressed by CpG methylation.
source: More than 70% of all human gene promoters contain stretches of CpG dinucleotides, termed CpG islands (CGIs), whose transcriptional activity is repressed by CpG methylation (Greenberg and Bourc'his, 2019; Weber et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: R-loops positioned near promoters of active genes maintain CGIs in an unmethylated state.
source: R-loops positioned near promoters of active genes maintain CGIs in an unmethylated state (Ginno et al., 2012), likely by reducing the affinity of DNMT1 binding to DNA (Grunseich et al., 2018), or recruiting ten-eleven translocation (TET) methylcytosine dioxygenases (Arab et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: TET enzyme family members share the ability to oxidize 5mC to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC).
source: The TET enzyme family members share the ability to oxidize 5mC to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) (Pastor et al., 2013; Tahiliani et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: 5hmC is a relatively rare DNA modification found across the genome much less frequently than 5mC.
source: 5hmC is a relatively rare DNA modification found across the genome much less frequently than 5mC (Mendonca et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Genome-wide, 5hmC is more abundant at regulatory regions near transcription start sites (TSSs), promoters, and exons, consistent with its role in gene expression regulation.
source: Genome-wide, 5hmC is more abundant at regulatory regions near transcription start sites (TSSs), promoters, and exons, consistent with its role in gene expression regulation (Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: The levels of 5hmC are enriched at active promoter regions, as observed upon activation of neuronal function-related genes in neural progenitors and neurons.
source: The levels of 5hmC are enriched at active promoter regions, as observed upon activation of neuronal function-related genes in neural progenitors and neurons (Pastor et al., 2013; Hahn et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: 5hmC has the potential to modify the DNA helix structure by favoring DNA-end breathing motion, a dynamic feature of the protein–DNA complexes thought to control DNA accessibility.
source: 5hmC has the potential to modify the DNA helix structure by favoring DNA-end breathing motion, a dynamic feature of the protein–DNA complexes thought to control DNA accessibility (Mendonca et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: 5hmC weakens the interaction between DNA and nucleosomal H2A-H2B dimers, facilitating RNA polymerase II elongation, and diminishes the thermodynamic stability of the DNA duplex.
source: Moreover, 5hmC weakens the interaction between DNA and nucleosomal H2A-H2B dimers, facilitating RNA polymerase II elongation, and diminishes the thermodynamic stability of the DNA duplex (Mendonca et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: While 5mC increases the melting temperature, 5hmC reduces the amount of energy needed to separate the two strands of the DNA duplex.
source: While 5mC increases the melting temperature, 5hmC reduces the amount of energy needed to separate the two strands of the DNA duplex (Leavitt et al., 2015; Wanunu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations revealed that the highest amplitude of GC DNA base-pair fluctuations is observed in the presence of 5hmC, whereas 5mC yielded GC base pairs (bp) with the lower amplitude values.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations revealed that the highest amplitude of GC DNA base-pair fluctuations is observed in the presence of 5hmC, whereas 5mC yielded GC base pairs (bp) with the lower amplitude values (Wanunu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: The presence of 5hmC destabilizes GC pairing by alleviating steric constraints through an increase in molecular polarity.
source: The presence of 5hmC destabilizes GC pairing by alleviating steric constraints through an increase in molecular polarity (Wanunu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Increased amounts of DNA:RNA hybrids were detected in samples derived from in vitro transcription of 5hmC-rich ACTB P1, ACTB P2, and APOE DNA templates.
source: In agreement with our hypothesis that 5hmC favors R-loops, increased amounts of DNA:RNA hybrids were detected in samples derived from in vitro transcription of 5hmC-rich ACTB P1, ACTB P2, and APOE DNA templates (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro transcription experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The S9.6 antibody equally recognizes DNA:RNA hybrids formed with C, 5mC, or 5hmC variants.
source: The S9.6 Ab was able to delay the run of the three substrates with similar kinetics, indicating that the Ab equally recognizes DNA:RNA hybrids formed with any of the three C variants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by EMSA experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: R-loop structures are more frequently formed in the presence of 5hmC as shown by atomic force microscopy.
source: In agreement with the hypothesis that transcription of 5hmC-rich DNA templates results in increased R-loop formation, AFM data revealed that R-loop structures are more frequently formed in the presence of 5hmC.
evidence: This is demonstrated by AFM imaging shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Replacing C by either 5hmC or 5mC significantly decreased the transcript levels in vitro.
source: These data show that the T7 polymerase is highly sensitive to DNA modifications since replacing C by either 5hmC or 5mC significantly decreased the transcript levels in vitro.
evidence: This is shown by RNA quantification from in vitro transcription experiments in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Depletion of Tet3 resulted in a significant loss of 5hmC in mES cells.
source: In contrast, depletion of Tet3 resulted in a significant loss of 5hmC, an effect that was exacerbated by the simultaneous depletion of the three enzymes (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by dot blot analysis in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No significant changes were observed in 5mC levels upon Tet depletion in mES cells.
source: No significant changes were observed in 5mC levels (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by dot blot analysis in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There is partial redundancy in the activity of the three Tet enzymes in mES cells.
source: This finding suggests that there is a partial redundancy in the activity of the three Tet enzymes in mES cells. The loss of Tet1 or Tet2 – but not of Tet3 – is compensated by the remaining Tets.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only Tet3 depletion reduces 5hmC levels.

claim: Dot-blot hybridization of total cellular nucleic acids using the S9.6 Ab revealed reduced endogenous R-loop levels in mES cells after depletion of Tet3 and after co-depletion of the three Tet enzymes.
source: In agreement with the hypothesis that 5hmC promotes R-loop formation, dot-blot hybridization of total cellular nucleic acids using the S9.6 Ab revealed reduced endogenous R-loop levels in mES cells after depletion of Tet3 and after co-depletion of the three Tet enzymes (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by dot blot analysis in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A significant reduction of 5hmC, but not 5mC, was obtained upon depletion of Tet3 and of the three Tets in mouse fibroblasts.
source: As observed in mES cells, a significant reduction of 5hmC, but not 5mC, was obtained upon depletion of Tet3 and of the three Tets in mouse fibroblasts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: This is shown by dot blot analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: The triple knockdown of the Tet enzymes significantly reduced the global levels of R-loops in mouse fibroblasts.
source: The triple knockdown of the Tet enzymes significantly reduced the global levels of R-loops in mouse fibroblasts, whereas Tet3 depletion in these cells had a minor impact in R-loops (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and D).
evidence: This is shown by dot blot analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and D.

claim: DRIP assays confirmed that R-loops are less abundant upon depletion of Tet enzymes.
source: The DRIP assays confirmed that R-loops are less abundant upon depletion of Tet enzymes.
evidence: This is shown by DRIP experiments in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Simultaneous depletion of the three Tet enzymes did not affect the expression levels of the analyzed genes in mES cells and mouse fibroblasts.
source: Importantly, simultaneous depletion of the three enzymes did not affect the expression levels of the analyzed genes in mES cells and mouse fibroblasts (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is shown by RT-qPCR analysis in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2F.

claim: The activity of Tet enzymes promotes the formation of R-loops in the absence of changes in transcription levels.
source: These data suggest that the activity of Tet enzymes promotes the formation of R-loops in the absence of changes in transcription levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Tet depletion reduces R-loops without affecting gene expression.

claim: Local enrichment of 5hmC following dCas9-TET1 targeting at the APOE locus was confirmed by DNA immunoprecipitation.
source: Local enrichment of 5hmC following dCas9-TET1 targeting at the APOE locus was confirmed by DNA immunoprecipitation using antibodies specific for 5mC or 5hmC-modified nucleotides (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown by (h)MeDIP experiments in Figure 2E.

claim: R-loop levels peaked significantly at the gRNAs-target and in the downstream region, upon tethering of dCas9-TET1 but not of dCas9-dTET1.
source: R-loop levels detected by DRIP peaked significantly at the gRNAs-target and in the downstream region, upon tethering of dCas9-TET1 but not of dCas9-dTET1 (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is shown by DRIP experiments in Figure 2F.

claim: The increased levels of R-loops detected far from the dCas9-TET1 target site are consistent with the view that R-loops have the capacity to extend from their inception locus.
source: The increased levels of R-loops detected far from the dCas9-TET1 target site are consistent with the view that R-loops have the capacity to extend from their inception locus. Accordingly, R-loops can be up to several hundred base pairs long and may extend over the entire gene body of shorter and/or highly transcribed genes (Sanz et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Editing 5hmC density by changing the expression levels or the genomic distribution of TET enzymes influences R-loop formation in cells.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that editing 5hmC density by changing the expression levels or the genomic distribution of TET enzymes influences R-loop formation in cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Computational analyses of 5hmC and R-loops datasets from mES and HEK293 cells revealed a marked overlap between 5hmC-rich loci and R-loops.
source: The resulting metagene plots and heatmaps revealed a marked overlap between 5hmC-rich loci and R-loops.
evidence: This is shown by computational analysis in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A statistically significant Pearson correlation coefficient between 5hmC and R-loops was obtained (p<0.05).
source: Despite the distinct distribution patterns of 5hmC (well-defined peaks) and R-loops (reads spanning genomic regions with highly heterogeneous lengths, ranging between a few dozen to over 1 kb Chen et al., 2015), we could obtain a statistically significant Pearson correlation coefficient between both (p<0.05) (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by correlation analysis in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Approximately half of all R-loops detected genome-wide occurred at 5hmC-containing loci.
source: Furthermore, approximately half of all R-loops detected genome-wide occurred at 5hmC-containing loci (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown by overlap analysis in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: An overlap between 5hmC and R-loops was observed in 6839 (51%) out of the 13,288 actively expressed genes.
source: Notably, we observed an overlap between 5hmC and R-loops in 6839 (51%) out of the 13,288 actively expressed genes (Figure 3D)
evidence: This is shown by gene-level overlap analysis in Figure 3D.

claim: Both 5hmC and R-loops increase towards the transcription termination site (TTS), where they reach maximum levels.
source: Metagene profiles revealed very similar patterns of intragenic distribution, with both 5hmC and R-loops increasing towards the transcription termination site (TTS), where they reached maximum levels (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown by metagene analysis in Figure 3F.

claim: At the TSS, 5hmC was mostly absent, whereas R-loops were abundant.
source: At the TSS, however, the 5hmC DNA modification was mostly absent, whereas R-loops were abundant.
evidence: This is shown by metagene analysis in Figure 3F.

claim: The detection of R-loop peaks at TSS regions implies that 5hmC is not necessary for co-transcriptional DNA:RNA hybridization and R-loop formation.
source: The detection of R-loop peaks at TSS regions is in agreement with previous studies (Ginno et al., 2013; Ginno et al., 2012) and implies that 5hmC is not necessary for co-transcriptional DNA:RNA hybridization and R-loop formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that R-loops are present at TSS where 5hmC is absent.

claim: TET1-KO human ES cells displayed significantly higher levels of readthrough transcripts genome wide when compared to wt human ES cells.
source: In agreement with a role in transcription termination, TET1-KO human ES cells displayed significantly higher levels of readthrough transcripts genome wide when compared to wt human ES cells (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is shown by transcriptome analysis in Figure 3G.

claim: Staining of mES cells with S9.6 and anti-5hmC antibodies gave rise to a robust PLA signal scattered throughout the nucleus, which was mostly lost after digestion of cells with RNase H.
source: Staining of mES cells with S9.6 and anti-5hmC antibodies gave rise to a robust PLA signal scattered throughout the nucleus, which was mostly lost after digestion of cells with RNase H (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by proximity ligation assay in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Metagene plots revealed marked enrichment of γH2AX at 5hmC-rich loci.
source: The resulting metagene plots revealed marked enrichment of γH2AX at 5hmC-rich loci.
evidence: This is shown by computational analysis in Figure 5A.

claim: Analysis of γH2AX and 5hmC distribution within active genes revealed a low yet statistically significant Pearson correlation coefficient (p<0.05).
source: Analysis of γH2AX and 5hmC distribution within active genes revealed a low yet statistically significant Pearson correlation coefficient (p<0.05) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown by correlation analysis in Figure 5C.

claim: 64% of all downregulated genes and 48% of all upregulated genes upon RNase H overexpression displayed R-loops overlapping with 5hmC.
source: Amongst the genes that were differentially expressed, we found that 64 and 48% of all downregulated and upregulated genes, respectively, displayed R-loops overlapping with 5hmC (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown by transcriptome analysis in Figure 6A.

claim: Pathway analysis revealed that differentially expressed genes with R-loops overlapping 5hmC are involved in the mTOR (downregulated) and MYC (upregulated) signaling pathways.
source: Pathway analysis revealed that these differentially expressed genes (Supplementary file 1) are involved in the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) (downregulated) and MYC (upregulated) signaling pathways (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is shown by pathway analysis in Figure 6B and C.

claim: mTOR and MYC are known to play opposite roles in establishing diapause, the temporary suspension of embryonic development driven by adverse environmental conditions.
source: mTOR and MYC are known to play opposite roles in establishing diapause, the temporary suspension of embryonic development driven by adverse environmental conditions (Fenelon et al., 2014), a stage that ES cells mimic when cultured in vitro.
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: mTOR, a major nutrient sensor, acts as a rheostat during ES cell differentiation and reductions in mTOR activity trigger diapause.
source: mTOR, a major nutrient sensor, acts as a rheostat during ES cell differentiation and reductions in mTOR activity trigger diapause (Bulut-Karslioglu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Overexpression of RNase H in mES cells did not reveal any significant changes in the cell cycle progression.
source: While overexpression of RNase H in mES cells did not reveal any significant changes in the cell cycle progression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: mES cells overexpressing RNase H displayed significantly decreased expression of genes related to pluripotency (Pou5f1) and germ layer commitment (Sox17, Sox6, Dll1) pathways.
source: we observed a significantly decreased expression of genes related to pluripotency (Pou5f1) and germ layer commitment (Sox17, Sox6, Dll1) pathways (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is shown by RT-qPCR analysis in Figure 6D.

claim: R-loops formed upon TET epigenetic reprogramming regulate gene expression in stem cells.
source: These data support the view that R-loops formed upon TET epigenetic reprogramming regulate gene expression in stem cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: 5hmC may impact R-loop formation by either destabilizing the DNA duplex or altering RNA polymerase II elongation rate.
source: Mechanistically, 5hmC may impact R-loop formation by either destabilizing the DNA duplex or altering RNA polymerase II elongation rate.
evidence: This is a mechanistic speculation based on known properties of 5hmC.

claim: 5hmC modifies the DNA helix structure by favoring DNA-end breathing motion, diminishes the thermodynamic stability of the DNA duplex, and destabilizes GC pairing.
source: Indeed, 5hmC modifies the DNA helix structure by favoring DNA-end breathing motion, diminishes the thermodynamic stability of the DNA duplex, and destabilizes GC pairing (Mendonca et al., 2014; Wanunu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: 5hmC weakens the interaction between DNA and nucleosomal histones, which is thought to accelerate RNA polymerase II elongation but can also facilitate nascent RNA annealing with the template DNA strand favoring R-loop formation.
source: It also weakens the interaction between DNA and nucleosomal histones (Mendonca et al., 2014), which is thought to accelerate RNA polymerase II elongation but can also facilitate nascent RNA annealing with the template DNA strand favoring R-loop formation.
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work and includes speculation about mechanisms.

claim: 5hmC-rich loci are hotspots for DNA damage genome-wide.
source: Indeed, we found that 5hmC-rich loci are hotspots for DNA damage genome-wide.
evidence: This is shown by analysis of γH2AX distribution in Figure 5.

claim: Genome-wide 5hmC and R-loops overlap robustly at the TTS of active genes.
source: Our findings that genome-wide 5hmC and R-loops overlap robustly at the TTS of active genes and that TET-deficiency drives transcription readthrough support a model whereby TET enzymes act upstream of R-loop formation during transcription termination (Skourti-Stathaki et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with citation to prior work on transcription termination.

claim: TET enzymes may play dual roles as both oncogenic and tumour suppressor genes.
source: TETs may play dual roles as both oncogenic and tumour suppressor genes, with the former arising as the consequence of altered expression levels or function, as observed in several cancers, such as triple-negative breast cancer (Bray et al., 2021; Good et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: TET-driven changes in the DNA methylation landscape may drive transcription-dependent genome damaging events that could facilitate cancer development and progression.
source: In addition to altering the expression levels of tumour suppressors or oncogenes (Bray et al., 2021), our findings suggest that TET-driven changes in the DNA methylation landscape may as well drive transcription-dependent genome damaging events that could facilitate cancer development and progression.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: A TET1 isoform that lacks regulatory domains, including its DNA-binding domain, but retains its catalytic activity, is enriched in cancer cells.
source: In agreement with this view, a TET1 isoform that lacks regulatory domains, including its DNA-binding domain, but retains its catalytic activity, is enriched in cancer cells (Good et al., 2017), suggesting that mistargeted TET activity may drive oncogenic events, such as genomic instability.
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: TET activity deposits 5hmC at DNA damage sites induced by aphidicolin or microirradiation in HeLa cells and prevents chromosome segregation defects in response to replication stress.
source: Conversely, TET activity deposits 5hmC at DNA damage sites induced by aphidicolin or microirradiation in HeLa cells and prevents chromosome segregation defects in response to replication stress (Kafer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: By driving the developmental DNA methylome reprogramming, TETs carry out numerous functions related to early developmental processes.
source: By driving the developmental DNA methylome reprogramming, TETs carry out numerous functions related to early developmental processes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: R-loops formed at 5hmC-rich regions impact the expression of genes involved in establishing diapause.
source: Our gene ontology analysis revealed that R-loops formed at 5hmC-rich regions impact the expression of genes involved in establishing diapause.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the pathway analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Changes in the activity of mTOR, a major nutrient sensor, control ES cell commitment to trigger diapause.
source: Accordingly, changes in the activity of mTOR, a major nutrient sensor, control ES cell commitment to trigger diapause (Bulut-Karslioglu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: The mTOR signaling pathway was significantly downregulated upon global R-loop suppression by RNase H.
source: The mTOR signaling pathway was significantly downregulated upon global R-loop suppression by RNase H.
evidence: This is shown by pathway analysis in Figure 6B.

claim: MYC targets, which prevent ES cells from entering the state of dormancy that characterizes diapause, were amongst the genes more significantly upregulated upon RNase H overexpression in mES cells.
source: Conversely, MYC targets, which prevent ES cells from entering the state of dormancy that characterizes diapause (Scognamiglio et al., 2016), were amongst the genes more significantly upregulated upon RNase H overexpression in mES cells.
evidence: This is shown by pathway analysis in Figure 6C with citation to prior work.
